Photograph: Russotwins/Alamy View image in fullscreen A ‘cluster’ of dead greater crested terns have been detected in south-west Victoria, the state government has announced. Photograph: Russotwins/Alamy Bird flu Suspected mass bird flu deaths found in second state as Murray Watt warns ‘this is the beginning’ Environment minister says Australia has ‘long and difficult journey’ and says more mass mortality events likely Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Lisa Cox and Petra Stock Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.13 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Aerial surveillance has detected mass bird deaths in a second Australian state in another suspected escalation of the spread of deadly H5 bird flu . The environment minister, Murray Watt, said on Monday Australia had begun “a long and difficult journey” as CSIRO analysis confirmed Australia’s first mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks off South Australia’s coast. Hours later, Victorian authorities said aerial observations had identified a “cluster” of dead and sick greater crested terns in the Glenelg River estuary near Nelson and across Lawrence Rocks, in the state’s south-west, over the weekend. If samples taken from the Victorian birds return positive results, it would be Australia’s second confirmed mortality event from the deadly disease that has devastated wildlife populations globally. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “I want to level with people: this is the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife,” Watt said on Monday. Aerial surveillance over Baudin Rocks identified about 50 dead and 30 sicks birds, the South Australian government said on the weekend. Samples taken from five greater crested terns and a silver gull were sent to the CSIRO’s Centre for Disease Preparedness and confirmed positive on Monday. “The reality is, you can’t stop native and wild birds flying around, and you can’t stop wild animals moving around, and that will mean more mass mortality events like the one we have now seen,” Watt said. View image in fullscreen Federal environment minister Murray Watt. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP “What we can do, and what we have been doing, is build up the resilience of the populations of our native birds and mammals.” In Victoria, the state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said aerial surveillance had made observations that were “consistent with what was recently reported in South Australia”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Read more Speaking to media on Monday afternoon, Cooke said aerial and ground surveillance in the south-west, near Portland and Nelson, in the past few days showed “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”. “Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change as the disease spreads out and has further impacts,” he said. The region is home to an important breeding colony of Australasian gannets as well as seal colonies and the Glenelg estuary and Discovery Bay, an internationally significant wetland site. South Australia’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said she was also concerned about a confirmed case of H5 bird flu in a petrel found in the Coorong, one of several new locations where the deadly disease has been detected in the state. The migratory petrel was one of 18 new cases in SA confirmed by CSIRO on Monday, which included the samples from six birds at Baudin Rocks. The new cases included a silver gull in Glenelg, two greater crested terns at Troubridge Island, a silver gull at Southend, a greater crested tern at Monarto and six greater crested terns on Pages Islands. The Coorong is a large area that is home to internationally significant wetlands that support populations of waterbirds and migratory species. “That confirmed location is of concern because it is where waterbirds are also located,” Bourke said “So it’s going from seabirds, but also potentially now into where we know a lot of waterbirds are nesting and using this space as a safe haven.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Victoria New South Wales Birds Wildlife news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Seven suspected new bird flu cases are ‘evidence of spread’ into Australian wildlife, experts warn Deadly H5 bird flu found in local Australian seabird for first time Bird flu?! https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: 1:35 Witnesses recount Christa Pike's survival of two lethal injections – video Tennessee Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder Christa Pike: what we know so far about Tennessee woman’s failed execution Richard Luscombe Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.44 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tennessee ’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her. Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville . Meanwhile, Pike, 50, remained in the hospital on Thursday afternoon. “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said at an afternoon press conference. “She is in critical condition receiving life-saving care. That is the extent of what we have at the moment.” Spivey, of the office of the post-conviction defender, condemned Tennessee authorities for the manner in which the failed attempt unfolded. He said officials used seven needles, one of which became bent as it was removed from Pike’s arm. “Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable,” he said, adding that he saw no life-saving care given after the execution attempt was abandoned at about 8.25pm. Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital. “This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened. 11:05 Death row inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections in Tennessee - The Latest “It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.” Lee added, in comments reported by the Tennessean , that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late Wednesday. “There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.” Cameron Sexton, the Republican speaker of Tennessee’s house of representatives, said on Thursday in a social media post that he and other lawmakers would also be investigating what went wrong with the attempted execution. He added that they would look at other ways to prevent executions from failing. “We will look at all options – expanding the alternatives, and changing the current medications to include potassium chloride,” he said. “Thirty years is too long for justice.” Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said her group was aware of seven other people that have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions. “This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she said in a statement. “What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes.” In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm. Pike, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing. Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt. “The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.” According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set. Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a livestream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time. They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out. John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.” Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull. Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied. Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year. Gary Wayne Sutton has been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December. https://www.ksl.com:443/article/51628420.text: LOGAN — Known as the coldest place in Utah every winter and one of the coldest places in the lower 48 states, Peter Sinks is now the focus of a Utah State University research project aimed at understanding why temperatures there drop so dramatically.Two USU researchers are gathering new data from the area, using additional weather sensors to study how cold air moves through the mountain basin and why it repeatedly becomes Utah's coldest spot.Peter Sinks is a natural limestone basin, shaped like a giant bowl, sitting at 8,164 feet in elevation. It has recorded some of Utah's most extreme cold temperatures for decades.It's not the only cold spot in the state. Nearby Lower Sink is a cold air pool basin, but smaller. Middle Sink is between the two, not too far off U.S. 89. It, too, traps cold air pools. But Peter Sinks is usually the coldest, about three miles off the highway and tucked in another basin.Peter Sinks has recorded extreme coldFeb. 1, 1985, the temperature at Peter Sinks plunged to 69.3 degrees below zero. That's the second-coldest temperature ever recorded in the lower 48 states. The lowest was -69.7°F at Roger's Pass, Montana, in January 1954. A sensor did record minus 70.5 degrees at Peter Sinks, but that reading was not considered official."Here is the Peter Sink, and here you can see our monitoring system," said Andras Dobos, a visiting scholar from Hungary, as he pointed to a laptop monitor.The researchers are studying what happens when cold air settles into the basin. For years, two weather stations have measured temperatures at the top of the rim of the basin, and another sensor at the bottom."And it's actually interesting because that's the deepest part. But oftentimes it's coldest here," said Timothy Wright, a graduate research assistant at USU, also pointing to a color-coded model on the laptop. Installing a new weather station at Peter Sinks Basin in northern Utah's Cache County.
